utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Would the registrar please bring in the accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And also bring in the witness at the same time. I would like to also say hello to everyone. Good morning to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If everyone can hear me, if everything is functioning properly, then we will continue with the cross-examination of Lieutenant-Colonel. Lieutenant-Colonel, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you rested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm rested, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you feel well? You are in your own country, so everything should be okay. Let us resume then. Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let us continue yesterday where we broke with Exhibit 416 which is the document titled "Call for Help" dated 4th of May, 1993, and authored by then Colonel Blaskic. If that could be provided to the witness in case he needs to refer to it? In looking at the document, I didn't find anything that suggested in it that Croats in Zenica should flee or evacuate. Do you have a contrary understanding of the contents of the document?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I see no order for Croats to flee, but then the title on top is a "Call for Help," not a call for flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So it was a call for assistance from the International Community in protecting Croats who were isolated to a greater or lesser extent in Zenica; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It's addressed to the U.N. High Commission of Refugees, and they are the organisation -- if any request is made, it should be made to this organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And is the request fairly characterised as a call for help to protect the Croat civilians remaining in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think the UNHCR is not the organisation to protect people, they are the organisation to provide help, to check on any threats made to certain populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's also addressed to the ECMM, the United Nations, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's right. But as I recall it, the mandate for the U.N. organisations at that time were only to provide security for UNHCR, and they did not have the clear mandate to provide security for any group of population at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And was that a source of frustration for both of the warring parties at times?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: As I recall it, both parties tried to get assistance from UNPROFOR and from other organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that the gist of this document is a request for help to protect Croats remaining in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I agree that this document is a request for help, but the facts listed in this document were not correct or at least not found to be true by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to the facts in the document. The document states in paragraph 1: "The difficult position of Croats in Zenica who have been living in total isolation for some time." Had the Croats in Zenica been cut off and isolated for some time as of the 4th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That question was asked yesterday and answered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I do not remember, really, very well. Perhaps I will call upon your memory, but if it has been stated that you have asked this question yesterday, then please go on to another question. Thank you, Judge Riad, for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will go forward, Mr. President. We only have limited time this morning, I know. If Exhibit 417 could be put before the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There's a redaction in the upper right-hand corner of the document. Do you know what's been redacted?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I tried to find the redaction on my own original, and I think it says Mr. Philip Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who redacted that or marked on that portion of the document?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know. I got this as a copy from the -- I think from the ECMM headquarters in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, this document was not addressed to the news media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: As far as I can tell from the distribution list, the news media are not on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So it went to international organisations?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, but I cannot tell whether it was distributed to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On its face, it went only to international organisations; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So when you described Exhibit 417 as propaganda, did you mean that Colonel Blaskic was trying to influence the views of international organisations present in Central Bosnia with respect to the plight of Croat people in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: According to my opinion, he is exaggerating the facts and he is trying to influence the international organisations that were working in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And with respect to this document, the reference to Kakanj, tell the court if Colonel Blaskic is exaggerating in this document events in Kakanj. What did happen in Kakanj on or about the 12th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: As I told you yesterday, I'm not fully aware of the events that happened in Kakanj since I left the scene at the 10th or 11th of June for a small vacation at the coast, and I came back in the area on the 16th or the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you think this document is an attempt to encourage Croat people in Vares -- excuse me, in Kakanj, to flee, or have they already fled Kakanj as of the 14th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness testified he did not and was not familiar with the events in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I asked him concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained. The witness did indeed answer you. He said very honestly that he did not have any details about the events in Kakanj. Please go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you have characterised this document as propaganda. Do you think this document was an attempt to encourage Croats to flee Kakanj? I'm not asking you about events in Kakanj. I'm asking you about the document. Was it an attempt by Colonel Blaskic to get Croats to flee Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm still not sure about fleeing from Kakanj, but I know that this fits into a pattern of exaggeration and a pattern of propaganda used by the HVO day after day. They sent a lot of messages like this to us ECMM, we used to discuss these messages in the evening meetings, and the general opinion of Mr. Thebault and also my opinion was that grave exaggeration was used as a propaganda to put influence on certain groups of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What group of Croats were the target, the influence, the group that was targeted for influence by Exhibit 417?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: As I read it, the number of Croats are referred to as people from Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So your testimony is this was an attempt to influence Croats in Kakanj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. He did not testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's a question.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: As I told you before, I am not familiar with the situation at Kakanj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please try to respond to the question.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I have read this article, this paper, this document as one document in a line of attempts to influence us as international organisations and to influence Croat people to come to certain Croat-held areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tell us, of the Croats in Central Bosnia who had to leave their homes, how many stayed in Central Bosnia and how many left Bosnia altogether? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know the exact numbers. I know that from certain areas around Zenica, in the beginning of my tour of duty, people fled to Grahovcici as I testified yesterday. A part of this group was brought back, the thing that we arranged. Later on, quite a large group fled from the area of Guca Gora in the direction of Novi Bila. I know of situations where a lot of Croats fled from the Travnik area and went to the Serb side, and after long travel, they came to another Croat-controlled or HVO-controlled area, and I was told by my own monitor that in the area of Kiseljak, a similar thing was prepared, that people from Kiseljak -- my own interpreter was a Croat girl living in the Kiseljak area. She and her family and other Croats had to be prepared to go to Ilidza, and as far as I know, Ilidza is a town in the centre of Sarajevo and was held by the Bosnian-Serb army. This all fits into a certain pattern that Croats either have to come to the HVO-controlled area or try to flee through Serb-held territory to another HVO-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We'll come back to this. But you said that your interpreter lived in the Kiseljak pocket or her family was there, and that there was an evacuation plan for Croats in the Kiseljak pocket in case it fell to the BiH army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's not what I said. Not in case it fell. She was told or her family was told by the Croat leaders, by the HVO leaders, to be prepared to evacuate to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To be prepared to evacuate the Kiseljak pocket to a location closer to Sarajevo outside of the pocket if necessary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think they should be prepared if necessary, yes, but I'm not aware of any threat on the Kiseljak pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, obviously someone viewed the Kiseljak pocket as threatened or else there wouldn't have been an evacuation plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, coming back to my earlier question. If you don't know, that's fine. Just tell us. But do you know: Did 185.000 Croats or more leave Bosnia, not for other HVO-held territories but for Croatia and the west as a result of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If Exhibit 418 could be put before the witness? This is the Mate Boban letter of 22 June, 1993, that you have characterised in the same vein, I believe, as Exhibits 416 and 417. Was this document on its face directed to the news media?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I cannot tell that from the face. On its face, it's directed to General Philip Morillon, UNPROFOR commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, tell us again how this came to you in the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Like I told you yesterday, I'm not sure whether I saw this one -- this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, perhaps you should avoid having the witness repeat himself, if you wish to gain some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. He said he wasn't sure. Yesterday I thought he said he saw it when he was an EC monitor in Central Bosnia, which I didn't understand how he would see General Morillon's personal correspondence at the time. He appears to be retracting from that statement, but I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I withdraw my own observation. This is in your interests, it is only in your interests that I make that comment. That's all. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether you saw this as an EC monitor or not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, there was a mix-up in numbers yesterday afternoon, and I referred to this one since I had it on my desk yesterday-- I'm not sure whether I saw this one in Bosnia or later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say "later on," in preparing for your testimony in the past few days?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did this document, on its face, is it copied to General Blaskic or the HVO authorities, the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I cannot tell from the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's not reflected on the heading that it was?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It's not reflected on the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The document on page 1 references a number of places, including Fojnica, that's about ten lines down under "Dear Sir." Do you know what happened to the Croat population of Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I visited Fojnica once, and that was in the end of May or the beginning of June, and there was nothing wrong in Fojnica. The army of BiH and the HVO were cooperative in that area by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There were joint civil authority structures in Fojnica, as you recall?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I only checked on the military structures, and they were joint military structures by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in Fojnica in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I read about it in the newspapers, but I wasn't there at that time. I think I left Bosnia already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And did you read that two days after General Morillon visited and proclaimed Fojnica a bright spot in an otherwise despairing situation, the BiH army attacked the Croats in Fojnica and drove them out and indeed they withdrew, causing a mass exodus of more than 5.000 Croats from Fojnica? Is that in substance what you read?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: The only thing I recall from reading the newspapers, the Dutch newspapers, was that the Dutch battalion gave assistance to a mental hospital and a kind of orphanage in Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You don't remember anything else?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's what I remember from the newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The same page implores General Morillon with respect to number of places, including Bugojno, asking that the same not happen there. What happened to the Croat population in Bugojno, do you know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It was not in my area of operations, it was in the same area of the British battalion, so I heard some things about what happened in Bugojno, but it was not my operation, and I did not visit Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Prior to your tour, were you briefed on events in the village of Dusina in the Zenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, I never heard that name before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you heard of the village Lasva in the Zenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I heard of a river called Lasva but not a village called Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about the village called Miletici?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I heard some allegations on a village called Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you visit this spot?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I did not visit it myself, but I know the allegations and I know that investigations have been done and that some of the allegations, as I recall it, a number of -- five or ten Croats have been killed in Miletici, allegedly by Muslim -- by the 7th Muslim brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This Boban letter references in the second paragraph promises made in a meeting held on June 10 in Medugorje. Do you know about that meeting, about any promises made in that meeting by General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I know the meeting taking place. I am not fully aware of the contents, I am not fully aware of the agreements made in Medugorje, because that was the beginning of my small vacation period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's turn to the issue of the responses to allegations of misconduct by the BiH army on the one hand and the HVO on the other. Would you agree that you did not have sufficient contact with either Colonel Blaskic or his counterpart General Hadzihasanovic in Zenica in order to judge their personal responses when news of improprieties or misconduct reached them?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, I had daily contacts with his representatives, so if they had thought it would be necessary for Mr. Blaskic to come with us, I think they would have advised him so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question was: Do you believe you have a basis to compare the personal responses of Colonel Blaskic with the personal responses of General Hadzihasanovic with respect to the issue of improprieties, crimes, and misconduct. If you do, please state, if not, please state?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I never met General Hadzihasanovic myself, I met Mr. Blaskic several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, General Hadzihasanovic had a staff, did he not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you meet them on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I met Mr. Merdan every day, almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Alagic, you spent time with Mr. Alagic, he reported to General Hadzihasanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think he did. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So are you saying that you can judge General Blaskic's responses to these types of issues -- excuse me, the then Colonel Blaskic -- but not General Hadzihasanovic, or do you have, in essence, an equal basis for judging both?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, as I told you, I never met Mr. Hadzihasanovic. It's hard to judge about his reactions. I met Colonel Blaskic several times, and I am sure that the things I reported during all the meetings were -- or at least could have been reported to Mr. Blaskic, and there were no reactions from the HVO side. The other thing is that we did not ask Mr. Alagic to come with us, he offered it himself, so it was his gesture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's talk about General Alagic's grand gesture regarding Guca Gora. You have testified that after you visited Guca Gora, the monastery was wrecked and desecrated, correct, in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Weeks after we first visited the church of Guca Gora, it was checked again, and then damage was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you talk to Alagic or anyone else in the BiH army then about this issue?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And what did they say?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: They showed that they were humiliated by that, and Alagic ordered -- or gave orders to BiH soldiers to clear up the mess.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And was anyone ever found responsible for the desecration and the destruction of the inside of the monastery?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I have no signs that anybody was punished for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever get a report from the BiH army or Mr. Alagic concerning his investigation?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I did not get a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When he told you it would be taken care of, did you trust him in that regard?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me read to you a portion of a report from the council of Europe, Parliamentary Assembly, dated 31 August, 1994, and ask you if you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. It would be helpful to the Prosecutor if we could have a copy of the same report that Counsel's reading from so we could take the statement that he's going to read to the witness, put it in proper context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hayman will give you a copy because even the Judges don't have one, so I assume that we're going to have something like this before you tender it; is that right, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not showing him the document. I'm going to ask him if he agrees with the statement. I'm going to read the entirety of the paragraph that begins "Guca Gora," it's a publicly available document, I don't have any copies. If the witness and the Prosecutor would like to look at it during the next break, he's free to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I think that's what we'll do. Maybe during the break, you can make some photocopies of that page, perhaps, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'll make it available for photocopies to be made, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, during the break, will a copy please be given to the Judges. Do you intend to tender it as evidence, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It depends on whether the witness agrees with the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. Very well. Then please read it slowly so that the witness will not be caught off guard. Thank you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Guca Gora: The civil and military BiH authorities in Travnik permitted the consultant to visit this site. The village, which contained many traditional farmhouses and buildings, was taken from the HVO, perhaps by Mujahedin soldiers, and it was ethnically cleansed of Croats with a lot of burning. Two weeks later, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina occupied the Franciscan monastery, which it still occupies."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question for you, Lieutenant-Colonel: Did General Alagic ever tell you that the monastery in Guca Gora became the BiH army headquarters in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, he did not tell me because I think it was not the fact when I was there in that period. I visited this monastery several times, and when I viewed it, it was not used as a BiH headquarters. And the other sentence about Mujahedin attacking and a lot of houses burning, that was not the case when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So when you left the theatre in July, the BiH army was not utilising the monastery?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. I did not visit Guca Gora the day when I left. I went several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When is the last time you visited?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think the end of June. I'm not sure about the date. The end of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that HVO authorities weren't responsive to allegations of improprieties and frequently attributed them to uncontrolled elements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask that a Prosecution Exhibit be put before you, 242, and that you be assisted in finding page D1 of Exhibit 242. 242, Mr. President, is an exhibit prepared by the ECMM, it's a report on inter-ethnic violence in Vitez, Busovaca, and Zenica, April 1993, and page D2 are the notes of the ECMM concerning an interview with General Hadzihasanovic, commander 3rd Corps, BiH army, held on 7 May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could find page D1?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I've got that page in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. The top of the notes indicate that the issue of hostages, which is an apparent reference to the kidnapping of commander Todic and other HVO officers in mid April 1993, was an issue raised with General Hadzihasanovic. And then if you look at the last two paragraphs of the notes, they read as follows, and this is attributed to General Hadzihasanovic: "It was best to go slowly. He wanted to have 7 Muslim brigade under control rather than not. The Mujahedin are not under control. There are many elements who are not controlled. He recommended I should meet one of his staff in the morning to go into detail." Now, is it your testimony you heard this type of representation from officers within the BiH army or you did not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm aware of the fact that when I arrived in theatre, the 7th Muslim brigade was not under control of the 3rd Corps army of BiH. Mr. Merdan told us several times. He also told us that he was desperately trying to get them under control, and he told us that he had achieved to do so -- I'm not sure when it was, but the end of May or the beginning of June, he said as of that moment, the 7th Muslim brigade was under his control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that before or after the Guca Gora mosque (sic) was desecrated and destroyed by the 7th Muslim brigade?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: The Guca Gora monastery was not devastated it was not destroyed. The 7th Muslim brigade came under their control a few days after the exchange of Mujahedin prisoners from Kaonik prison, and the Croat colonels and some other Croat officers. I'm not sure when that was. I can look it up in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's in May, middle of May, something like that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: So at the end of May then, they came under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said in your direct testimony that Mr. Nakic and Mr. Merdan's orders were obeyed. Are you qualifying that earlier testimony by saying now to the Court that prior to the end of May, the BiH army and General Merdan did not have control over the 7th Muslim brigade and his orders would not have been obeyed and respected by the 7th Muslim brigade?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, according to my opinion, in the Dutch army, you cannot give orders to units that are not under your command. So it's not a matter of disobeying orders, they were just not under the command of third Muslim -- of the third BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So General Merdan told you that he wasn't attempting to give orders to the 7th Muslim brigade because he felt he could not control them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: He told me that he was attempting to get them under his control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And how do you do that if you don't attempt to give direction, including orders, to a unit?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether they were in his order of combat, I mean, in the hierarchy of the 3rd corps, or maybe they changed a commander or punished somebody, I'm not sure about that, but the fact is that after the exchange of prisoners, this Muslim brigade was reported to us as being under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At the end of May?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: At the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You discussed the relative levels of destruction to Muslim religious sites and Catholic religious sites in Central Bosnia. Have you undertaken a study of that question or is your testimony anecdotal in nature?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I did not make a special study on that subject myself. I think I can state this opinion by everything I saw in theatre, and I can state it by the discussions we had at ECMM and BRITBAT headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me just test the breadth of your experience by mentioning a few locations and ask you if you ever visited them or heard of them. The monastery in Doboj (phoen) Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of Doboj in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The church in Cep near Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I visited the church in Cep near Kacuni, and I did it together with the priest from Busovaca, we escorted him, and there the priest showed us that some of the sacred Catholic things, like the box where they keep the sacramental wafers, this box was forcefully opened, and the sacramental wafers were thrown on the ground. That is felt as a desecration of holy Catholic objects, and we cleared up the mess together with this party that visited the church. The church itself was not damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it later damaged much more severely, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Not during the period I visited that area because I used to drive along that church when I had to go to the Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you know the church in Proseje was burned?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Can you tell me where that is, this town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It would help me if I can see it on the map, because I'm familiar with most names in the area where I worked, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We'll find it --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Normally I use a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We'll find it on a map during the next break. The church in Borovici near Vares?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I never visited that church in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The monastery in Klarisa (phoen) near Brestovsko (phoen)?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I never was in Brestovsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said in Grahovcici, the 2nd corps allowed a meeting and that was indicative of their positive attitude. Could you explain that comment? I didn't understand it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I said the 2nd corps because it doesn't sound familiar to me, I don't think there was a 2nd corps there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I didn't think so either. The BiH army then. You said some kind of a meeting was allowed in Grahovcici, and that was indicative of a positive BiH army attitude. Can you add to that comment?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think you are referring to my visit at Grahovcici at the beginning of -- no, at the end of April when I assisted Father Stjepan in investigating in the area and in convincing the Croats that it was safe for them to go back to their own houses. This assistance made by the 3rd corps was in that way that they allowed us to pass checkpoints to allow us to cross the frontlines and to go into HVO-held territory. And later on, in the second phase of our operation, they assisted us with providing buses, in the beginning they provided an ambulance but took it back later on because Zenica was under artillery attack, and they provided military police escorts as far as the latest BiH checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for explaining your earlier comment. You described being blocked at an HVO checkpoint trying to evacuate wounded from Travnik on a particular occasion. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about that. Did you have permission from the 3rd corps and the HVO operative zone for that evacuation and nonetheless you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. This was an evacuation prepared during one of the meetings, during one of the local commission meetings were brigade commanders usually were present, and they assured us that we could take a number of wounded people from the Travnik hospital, and this was a mixed number of people, so civilians and soldiers, Croat soldiers and Muslim soldiers, Croat civilians, Muslim civilians, women and children, a number of 18 altogether. We prepared this very thoroughly with help of Dr. Mirsad Granov, they selected the most severely wounded people for us, and everybody agreed in passing the checkpoint, everybody agreed in us evacuating these wounded people to Zenica hospital where they could get better treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And yet either the order didn't get passed down to the checkpoint or the soldiers at the checkpoint didn't obey that order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Am I correct in concluding that during your tour of duty, you did not receive any reports of investigations into atrocities or misconduct from either army, BiH army or HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Most of the allegations of atrocities were from the BiH side in the direction of the Croats. We did a lot of investigations ourselves, and we asked both sides to do their investigations from their side, and we did not get results from -- on that request. If I compare them, I think we did at least ten times more requests through the HVO side than to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I take it your answer is yes, you did not receive any reports of investigations from --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: We did not receive any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would that be normal, that an army would not give out internal reports of investigations to outside parties, such as internal (sic) organisations? Would the Dutch army do that as a matter of course, give out internal investigative reports?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Depends on what it is. If there is a normal military operation, you wouldn't report on that operation to foreigners, to outsiders, but if there's an incident like a truck bomb, then I would be very keen on investigating that and reporting to anybody who would like to know it. Because reporting is the only chance to get the burden off your back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, ECMM did an investigation into the shelling of Zenica on the 19th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that was a written report? Was it a written report --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It's a report made by Mr. Lars Baggesen, one of my colleague monitors, and an investigation into the shelling was done during the period I was in Vitez or the ECMM house in BRITBAT.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether that report was made available to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was made available, but all the findings of the ECMM were usually discussed during the joint operation command meetings or during the old Busovaca Joint Commission meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have no knowledge that the report was made available; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I personally have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many times was Zenica shelled during your ten- or eleven-week tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It was shelled very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You also said that you were denied entry into Gomionica in the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Prior to going, and while I'm asking this, could Exhibit 93 be retrieved? Prior to going, do you have approval from the HVO operative zone to go into the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. Prior to going, we went to the Kiseljak headquarters, we met Mr. Bradara there, we told him that we would go to Rotilj to investigate on allegations, and that after that, we would go to Gomionica, and he told us that he agreed on that and he would prepare safe passage for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yet you went to Gomionica and you were stopped by a squad of HVO soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. We were stopped by a single HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And did he tell you that his commander Ivica Rajic (phoen) had given orders to stop all UN, UNHCR, and ECMM vehicles? If you need to refresh your recollection, that statement is in the middle of your report which is Exhibit 93, about the eighth or ninth line down.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what I reported in my special report of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, elsewhere in your statement to the Prosecutor's Office, you identified Mijo Bozic as the brigade commander in Kiseljak, is that correct, Mijo Bozic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't recall that I used his name before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who was the brigade commander in Kiseljak during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning it was Mr. Rajic, but he was told (sic) to be killed at the frontlines, and later Mr. Bradara introduced himself as being the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was this incident -- I'm sorry. The dates on your reports are somewhat difficult for civilians to comprehend. Can you help me? What was the date of your visit?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I have to look it up in my book, but the date when this report was sent was the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. As of the 27th of April, had Mr. Rajic been killed on the front-line yet, or was he still in command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I have to look it up. But I think when I reported in this way, then that's what the soldier at the front-line told me, that his commander, Rajic, apparently was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And your understanding was if Rajic was alive and was his commander, he would have been the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, he would have been the brigade commander. But if his deputy or his second in command or the one who introduced himself as the actual brigade commander tells us that we can go anywhere we like and that it's free for us to investigate in Rotilj and in Gromiljak, then I think there's good grounds for us to believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And it tells you, does it not, that something is wrong, when you go to the brigade headquarters, they tell you you have permission to go, and yet when you go to the village, a soldier blocks you and says someone else gave him an order to block you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's right, but that's an excuse often used by soldiers, that somebody else told him not to let us through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So what do you think? Do you think this was a deception by Mr. Bradara or what? What are you telling this Court? Or do you know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe it's a miscommunication, maybe it's a deception. I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So on this particular day, the HVO wasn't so well-organised and well-functioning; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That might be true. I cannot say from the facts. The only thing I can say is that we were stopped there and that one of the top level officers in the headquarters of Kiseljak, HVO Kiseljak, told us that we were free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You've said that. Thank you. Let's turn to the subject of interference with aid. You saw the Convoy of Joy interfered with. Where did you see the Convoy of Joy?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I saw the Convoy of Joy heading for the coast, hundreds of trucks, and I saw it coming back. I didn't see the interference myself, but I saw the results of it. And the results were that in the area of Novi Travnik and -- a lot of trucks were damaged, that some trucks were held in HVO-held territory, that some trucks were looted, some other trucks were hidden behind a church in Rankovici, and we spoke to the priest about those trucks hidden behind the Catholic church, and he told us that these trucks were meant to go to the area north in Bosnia, and that he saved those trucks from the looting. There were clear signs of robbed trucks, all kinds of things, clothing and pieces of food lying on the ground. Later on we found trucks in Busovaca, we found four drivers belonging to the Convoy of Joy in Busovaca. They stated that they didn't dare to go on anymore, and that they lost their trucks and their cargo. I wrote in my diary that we did not believe them at that time because we thought they had sold their goods in Croat-held territory. That's what I know about the Convoy of Joy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, my question was: Where did you see it? And we will be able to conclude this morning if you focus on my question. On redirect, you can give any additional details that the Prosecutor invites. I take it you didn't see it until after it was broken up, and then you saw some trucks in different places; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know on whose orders or direction the Convoy of Joy was commandeered?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: The Convoy of Joy was arranged by, as far as I know it, by the joint command in Travnik, they had a special officer to arrange this Convoy of Joy, a Colonel Siber, and they asked for support several times, and as far as we were allowed and we were capable, we supported them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who directed the robbing of the convoy, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether Colonel Blaskic attempted to free and recover the convoy?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's turn to Kruscica. You said a second road was opened for you after Colonel Blaskic wrote his order which is Defence Exhibit 141. What do you mean, a road was opened for you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: There apparently was a parallel road to the main road, and at the base of the road, as we drove by, there was an HVO-manned military roadblock opened for us to be able to pass, so I pulled off the road--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request that there be a break between questions and answers for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was this roadblock that had existed essentially on the front-line, was it on the front-line in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: You cannot say that the roadblock is exactly on the front-line. The roadblock is that far away from the front-line so there is no direct fire on the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The last presence of the HVO before no man's land, is that right? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I would say that it's the last safe place. Soldiers on the front-line always move a little bit further, so there's no direct fire on the roadblock, soldiers on the front-line can receive direct fire and they should be able to give direct fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You had had permission, authority, and so forth from the Vitez brigade to go into Kruscica before you received Defence Exhibit 141; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: We discussed this matter with Mario Cerkez several times, and we discussed it in the local commission Vitez several times where his representatives were present, and the answer we got almost after every request was that the road was blocked by angry civilians and that they could not control these angry civilians. Nevertheless, we tried to force our way through this human blockade, and we failed in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Had there been any discussion about an alternate route before the occasion when you went in through an alternate route?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: We were not aware of that alternate route, so we didn't ask for it. I think the people at the ground, living in their own community should be aware of an alternate route.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said your life was threatened by an HVO soldier at the Novi Bila hospital. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that threat reported to the Vitez brigade or the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. I reported it myself during one of the local commissions Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To ...

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: To the officer present at that time. I'm not sure whether it was Mario Cerkez himself, Mr. Borislav Jozic was present at all those meetings, so he must have been there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Borislav Jozic, was he killed by a sniper in Stari Vitez during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: He was killed after I left the scene. I was told by a colleague monitor in a private letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn he was killed by a sniper in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I was told that he killed -- he was killed in the area of Vitez. They didn't write to me whether it was done by a sniper or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's turn to Busovaca and the four trucks of medical aid and powdered milk. Exhibit 421 may be helpful to your testimony. If it could be provided to the witness? 421. I would first direct your attention to paragraph 4. During most of your testimony yesterday, you referred to the police commander as a chief of police or commandant of police, but, in fact, he was the commander of the military police, the HVO military police, based in Busovaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And is it also correct that the convoy was hijacked apparently by local soldiers from Busovaca and then taken into the custody of the military police?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. I was not present when it was hijacked. That's what I was told by the drivers and later on by the commander of the police himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is the contents of paragraph 5 correct, wherein it discusses the fact that the papers for the cargo were not in proper order?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, but the meaning of that is that the drivers took some goods with them for their private use, like a small gas burner to heat up their own food they needed during the road, and those small things. Maybe 1 per cent of the cargo was not on the cargo list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the rest of paragraph 5, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 13, you discuss the linkage issue, which I still don't understand. I apologise for that. Did the issue of the roadblock arise when two BRITBAT Warriors came down the road and ran into the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, it did not. The BRITBAT Warriors were already in Busovaca when I arrived. I tried to go with my own car, my armoured Mercedes from Zenica, using the normal road along the Lasva Valley, and we were stopped at this roadblock, it was unmanned, there was a large lorry blocking the road, and mines around this lorry, so we had to return to Zenica, and then asked for permission to use the road, the mountain road from Zenica through Botajica (phoen), Grabovica, and then to Busovaca. The warriors came from the British battalion. They were already in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What is it that Mr. Grubesic said he wanted done or not done with respect to that lorry. What was linked to the issue of the medical supplies and trucks?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: What was linked? That he asked us to take away the threat coming from Zenica, military threat on Busovaca. That was the reason why they put the roadblock there. If we were able to take that threat away, then he would give us back the trucks and the cargo and the drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But, of course, you're not able to take away the threat from the 3rd corps?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's clear. We were not a party in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So basically he told you, "No, we're not giving you back the cargo"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: You could make that out of his words, but he did not say that literally, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to learn that Colonel Blaskic had ordered that roadblock be cleared?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I'm surprised by that because the next day the truck was taken away but then there was a large crater in the road, so there was even a larger roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now I understand. Very well. Thank you. Now I have a question about what this military police commander in Busovaca told you, and this is very important to the Defence, so please listen carefully. Did this military police commander tell you that on the second day -- July 2nd, 1993, that you came to discuss the issue of the medical supplies, that you would have to come back later because he had to ask permission from his superior in Mostar before acting on this matter?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. We had a long discussion with this chief of military police at the 2nd of June, and at the end of the day, he gave us the impression that everything could be arranged. The only thing he needed was permission from his chief in Mostar, and that we should come back the next day, that's the 3rd of June. That's what we were prepared for, to do on the 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you understood him to be referring to the chief of the overall military police of the HVO in Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, hearing him speaking as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are we talking about June or July? Which month is it? You mentioned 2nd of July, then I heard you mention the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's 2nd July, Mr. President. I'm sorry if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue. That's very clear. So you said you had to come back on the 3rd of July. I understand now. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Hearing this man in his uniform, police uniform, speaking to us, referring to his chief, then it's clear for us that his chief must be a policeman as well, a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask the technical booth now to assist? I'd like to play a few seconds of Exhibit 270, a videotape, and we'll try to freeze the videotape on a particular individual, and my question for you will be whether you can identify the military police commander in Busovaca, the individual you dealt with in connection with this convoy, on the videotape. So if the videotape could commence? I'm not seeing it on my screen. Maybe it's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This tape, Mr. President, is a Prosecution Exhibit. It's a videotape taken on the night of the 16th of April, 1993, in the bungalow in Nadioci adjacent to Ahmici after the action in Ahmici on 16 April. If we could freeze the tape there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that individual in the bungalow on the 16th of April as the same military police commander who told you his chief was in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: He looks like the picture that was shown to me yesterday that I identified as Mr. Ljubesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It looks like the same man?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It's hard to say in a dark surrounding like this, but it looks like the same man. Same eyebrows, same nose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday with the Prosecutor you reviewed four orders of Colonel Blaskic which you obtained from BRITBAT, I believe, in the course of your tour of duty. Those are defence 141, Exhibit 422, 423 -- excuse me. That's 423 and 424. It occurs to me, Mr. President, if a still could be made from the freeze frame of Exhibit 270 and marked as the next exhibit in order, that would be helpful. You said, Lieutenant-Colonel, that these four orders were well organised and well-written professional military orders; is that true?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And we can deduce from that, and this Court should deduce from that, should it not, that these orders were written by a trained military officer?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond that, can you deduce from the orders themselves the quality of reports that may have been received in return, or even whether proper reports were received in return?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I cannot tell from this order because it's the first order I saw, and I'm aware of, that his subordinates were ordered to report back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Those are matters, I take it, that are internal to an armed force and generally aren't shared with outside entities?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That depends on whether it's normal military activity that's not spread outside, and if it concerns violations of humanitarian laws, then I think it should be reported to ECMM, to UNHCR, and to the British battalion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tell me, from the lower level commanders in the HVO you encountered, were they professional career military officers? Take Mario Cerkez, for example. Was he a career officer?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you think he had been to military academy?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not aware if there's a military course like that in the former Yugoslavia, but I think he was trained and it was his normal professional job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to learn he was trained in the area of mechanics or mechanical, you know, machines?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm surprised by that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about Mr. Grubesic, the brigade commander in Busovaca? Was he a career professional military officer; do you know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. He made a less professional impact on me, and I state that because of this picture shown to me yesterday where he wears a red beret in a way a professional soldier should not wear his beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He had been an auto mechanic before the war, had he not? Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, I did not learn that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn what -- excuse me. Did you learn what his occupation had been?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the case of each of these orders, you were asked by the Prosecutor whether these orders referenced higher orders or agreements between the parties, and you said "Yes." If a commander repeatedly and of his own initiative orders and reminds subordinates of their obligations under international law and the laws of war, what would that say about that commander to you, as opposed to a commander who only passes down orders from his superiors?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: If there was any need to do it repeatedly, then it would show to me that he did not have full control of his -- over his subordinates, but this was the first time it was reported to us, and we discussed these matters of violations of humanitarian law almost every day, and since this is reported on the 19th of June, I was in theatre for more than two months then reporting it every day, so that's 50 or 60 times, there was no answer, no reply, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the question you have in your mind, I take it, is why weren't these things ordered sooner?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Why didn't they show us that they ordered these things?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, Mr. President? This is an exhibit, Mr. President, which is the first in a series of exhibits. They are orders of General Blaskic. They consist, at least most of them, of an original B/S/C copy, a French translation, I'm pleased to say, and an English translation, and I would ask they be marked as the next exhibit in order, with the French designated as the "A" Exhibit and the English as the "B" Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is this right? Will the French take the letter "A" Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: When possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. I'm very happy about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have noticed that, Mr. President. May I inquire what the number of this first exhibit will be of the registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document D147.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could take a moment, Lieutenant-Colonel, to examine the exhibit. It's short. This is just to summarise, briefly, this is an order issued on the 27th of April, 1993, by Colonel Blaskic to the commander of the Vitez brigade, supplementing an earlier order of the 24th of April, prohibiting any treatment of temporarily detained civilians contrary to the basic provisions of the Geneva Convention. Is this an order that, on its face, was done at the self-initiative of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It's a supplement to another order, so I can't tell for sure, but reading it from these few lines, there is no sign that it is based on another order, but it's still a supplement to an order number from the 1st of April -- the 24th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What would it tell you if Colonel Blaskic was repeating an order three days later that he had previously given on the 24th of April? Does that tell you that there was a need, over a period of only 72 hours, to repeat and reinforce an order to a brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think so, yes. There was a need then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist once again? We have an improved translation, Mr. President, of what had been marked as Exhibit D43, the English translation has been redone by the translation unit, and I think it's improved over the original provided by the Office of the Prosecutor, and so I would like to have it marked as a new exhibit and shown to the witness. Again, it's in triplicate, three languages. I believe this will be Defence Exhibit 148, 148A, and 148B.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could find the English copy, Lieutenant-Colonel, I'll direct you to it. It also is an order of Colonel Blaskic to multiple brigades and special purposes units and others regarding treatment of citizens' personal property, and it reads in the opening line: "In order to stop arson attacks on houses and business premises as well as the looting of property, I hereby order" -- and the order includes paragraph 1 on the territory of the area of responsibility of the Central Bosnia operative zone command controlled by the HVO --"I most strictly forbid the torching of houses and business premises and the looting of property." Is this an order that you came into possession of during your tour in Central Bosnia or indeed prior to your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't recall that I saw this order before, at least not that I got it in the area, and I cannot tell because normally I used to read the English first, so I don't know whether the first translation is available. Maybe I can recognise it from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit D43 could be provided to the witness, perhaps he can recognise the earlier version of the translation. D43.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the same document except there are no references there to the D43 on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand that comment, Mr. Registrar. Is it the wrong exhibit or is it the same?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The question is, if it could be shown to the witness so that he can determine if it's a document, the English version of which he may have seen in the theatre at the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, I do not recall that I saw this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On its face, was this an order merely handing down or repeating the order of a superior commander, or was it an order taken on the initiative by Colonel Blaskic, by his own self-initiative?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say so in the heading that he is basing this on another order and he doesn't -- doesn't either say that he's repeating it. He orders it in a clear way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask for the registrar's assistance for another order in this series. If the registrar could assist? This, I believe, will be D149, 149A and 149B. Lieutenant-Colonel, regrettably the translation we obtained of this does not include the full heading -- wait a minute, I'm sorry, I may have misspoken. Yes, it does. The English translation is spread out over three pages, and this order is dated 24 April, 1993, titled "Position on Housing and Property in Flats," it was issued to multiple units, and included the police station in Vitez and the chief of police in Travnik in which the accused recites initially: "In view of the large number of flats which have been temporarily abandoned and are being forcibly entered by armed individuals, HVO soldiers and other persons, and with the aim of increasing the quality of public peace and order in the town of Vitez and other towns /added in handwriting / and preventing these negative occurrences, I hereby order: (1) Use all means necessary and in extreme cases use force to prevent the usurpation of housing space and appropriation of property from flats belonging to citizens who are temporarily and under various conditions" -- let me confer with my colleague. There's a word, Mr. Nobilo advises me, that the word "absent" should appear, at least in the English translation in paragraph 1, and we will look into that, Mr. President. And then the order continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: First, Lieutenant-Colonel, this order being directed to the civil police, is that normal? What does that tell you, if the civil police are being called to action to protect private property and prevent, quite frankly, Muslim apartments from being confiscated and Muslims from being forced from their flats?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any civil police force still in action, still being in action in Vitez, I never saw any civil police, but if he addresses an order to the civil police, I suggest they are still there. But they never showed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They were not much of a presence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I never met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was this an order, on its face, merely repeating or passing down the order of a superior command, or does it appear to have been taken on the initiative of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It doesn't say so in the heading that it's based on another order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is this an order you saw in the theatre?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tell us, at this time, the 22nd to the 26th or 27th of April, 1993, was the HVO under extreme pressure because of attacks by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: What period again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Roughly the 22nd, 20th or 22nd of April to the 26th or 27th of April, that week.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any severe pressure on the HVO positions, but that was the period when I was active in Grahovcici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask for the assistance then of the usher? This exhibit, Mr. President, is a protest from Colonel Blaskic concerning BiH army attacks in violation of the cease-fire that had been agreed to at the time in the area of Kuber Mountain and elsewhere. It will be marked, I believe, as Exhibit D150, 150A, and 150B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps we will now take a break, Mr. Hayman. This will give you the time to distribute these documents. Before the break, however, I'd like to make some point about how we're going to organise our work. We're going to be stopping at 1.00 p.m. How much more time do you think you will need, Mr. Hayman? Do you think you will need to use the entire rest of that time? Don't forget, there may be questions from the Prosecution as well, and also the Judges will have questions. Otherwise, the Colonel will have to come back another time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am cognisant of that, and I do want to help all of us finish this session. I estimate I have one more hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will take a 15-minute break, but I doubt that we'll be able to end this morning. I think given the fact that we have very little time, we'll have to stop at 1.00 p.m., and we'll simply have to bring the witness back when it is necessary to do so. I don't think there is anything else to state. I have no power nor wish on my part to restrain you in the questions you wish to put. You are at liberty to put the questions you wish. I try to cut any repetitions or cut any lengthy answers, but this is how things are. So let us now take a break, and we will take a 20-minute break because the interpreters need a 20-minute break, and then if there are any questions left, we will have those questions, then go on to the next session when the witness can come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Tribunal is now in session. Would the accused please be brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Hayman. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, we were looking at Exhibit D150. Does this refresh your memory concerning events during the time period, roughly the 22nd of April, for the following week concerning the level of activity and fighting between the BiH army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Reading this protest, I'm aware of the fact that there were cease-fire violations in the area of Kuber, which I referred to in this document. There were a lot of cease-fire violations from both sides in the entire area, and I know there have been made a lot of protests on these cease-fire violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know where Kuber Mountain was?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I know where it was. Between Zenica -- it's the high ridge between Zenica and the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that whoever held Kuber Mountain held the dominant high ground between Zenica and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It depends on what kind of weapons you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that Kuber Mountain was a very important military site in the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And it was taken by the BiH army; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not aware whether it was taken or whether they had it in their possession already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But it was under their control at least by the end of your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It has been -- according to my knowledge, it has been under their control for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see this protest during your tour of duty? It's addressed to the ECMM Zenica, and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I did not see it during my duty there. I'm aware of the facts that are described in this document, and I recall that they were discussed during one of the ECMM meetings in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know whether, when violations of Colonel Blaskic's orders came to his attention, did he follow up? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I know that we reported violations or discussed violations almost every day during our local commission meetings, and we were not reported by any action coming from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So his follow-up, if there was follow-up, was a private matter within the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: If there was any follow-up, it was a private matter. We never got reports on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist and distribute D151? This only exists at this moment, Mr. President, in B/S/C. We'll have to put it on the ELMO and deal with it as best we can. It's been provided to the interpreters in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So if we can put it on the ELMO and, Lieutenant-Colonel, we can all listen while my colleague describes the date heading and reads the critical portion of the order. I'm not asking him to read it in its entirety to save time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document D151.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It's an order of the operational zone Central Bosnia from the 30th of May, 1993, and the order has been given to the command of the military police of the 4th battalion Vitez and to the assistance of the security and information unit, and the title is "Existence of Behaviours Contrary to the Orders and Operational Tasks." "On the day of the 30th of May, the person on duty of the operational zone Central Bosnia has reported that members of the military police, Mr. Franjo Ramljak and Mr. Slavko Hrgic, are forcibly expelling Muslim families despite the order which prohibited to do the above-mentioned actions, and for which the above-mentioned gentlemen were responsible with regard to the execution. "In order to prevent any other actions that jeopardise the implementation of the order and correct behaviour of the military police members during the execution of the ordered tasks, I order: Firstly, to investigate this case and enforce disciplinary measures against the perpetrators of this action. Report to me why individual members of your unit, despite continuous warnings and instead of maintaining public order, persistently commit misdeeds and what to do to prevent further occurrences." The date for the implementation of this order is the 5th of June, 1993; the signature of Colonel Blaskic and the seal of the operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: First let me ask you, this is directed in its first line I believe to the commander of the 4th Vojne, Vojne Policije in Vitez. Do you know whether that is the same individual you dealt with in Busovaca from the military police?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
