utterances.text: I'm not sure that the military police commander in Busovaca was the battalion commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If he was, then this would be addressed in part to the same individual; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What does it tell you if -- you've seen the prior orders issued by Colonel Blaskic concerning the protection of apartments and flats and so forth. What does it tell you that one of the units empowered to implement the prior order is now, apparently, not only not enforcing the prior order but perpetrating violations of it to the point where Colonel Blaskic has to act? Does that tell you that his orders are not being faithfully carried out by this particular unit, the 4th Vojne of the Vojne Policije?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It tells me that he is reacting on certain violations, but it also tells me that this 4th battalion is under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tell me, if a unit had dual lines of command, that is, one to a geographic zone commander but also to another command, such as the military police commander in Herzegovina, would it be incumbent on the geographic commander, when he learned of a violation, to do his best to enforce discipline and enforce control over that unit even if that unit had two lines or chains, if you will, of command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I cannot believe that there were really two lines of command. In a war zone, there's only one commander. That's the theory that's used in -- I think in every army, there's one chain of command, there's one top commander in the area. There might have been a second chain, but then probably an administrative chain. I cannot believe that there are two commanders in one area. It's impossible to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tell us: Did you discuss this subject with the Prosecutors during the break?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I did not discuss this subject of two commands. It's -- really, it's my personal opinion. It's impossible to use -- to work, to operate with two commanders. We discussed the subject about whether it was operational or technical command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With respect to the Vojne Policije?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: With respect to the 4th battalion as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the subject of civilians digging trenches. You went to Skradno with members of the local joint commission to investigate this issue; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. The local joint commission Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As a result of that meeting, did the HVO in Skradno agree not to use civilians in that form of work?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: The allegation was made several times, and that was the reason why we went to Skradno and talked to the people in Skradno, and they were the ones who told us that it still went on, and we tried to react on that again, but it's hard to get concessions from one of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the joint commission member from Busovaca on behalf of the HVO present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: There were two members present, one in civilian clothes, an older man with a bald head, and there was one of the military members present. I've got a picture of that meeting, so I'm very sure who was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was the position or role of the civilian?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: He was, as I recall it, one of the members of the civil government of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he have a civil defence function?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. After a while, working in Busovaca, we introduced the civil government from both sides, including the Catholic priest and the imam from the area of Busovaca, to bring some more trust amongst parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did one or both of the HVO or Croat joint commission representatives tell the HVO in Skradno that they were not to compel civilians to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: The HVO Skradno was not present during this visit. We visited these people in their own houses or in the houses where they lived together with relatives or friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said in your prior statement that on the 12th of May, "We got agreement from the HVO at Skradno to stop the use of civilians to dig trenches." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: As I recall it now, it was in Stranje, that's the small village on the other side of the village -- the other side of the river, approximately one kilometre from Skradno.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It was in Stranje that agreement was obtained to stop the practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In Stranje, did the joint military members, either civil or military from Busovaca, on behalf of the HVO and the civil Croat government, did they tell the HVO in Stranje that they were not to engage in this practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know, since the -- only the discussions I personally had with Croat or Muslim people were translated by my interpreter, and she didn't used to translate all the other conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you recall any particular occasion when the allegation of forcible trench-digging by civilians, Muslim civilians, was raised with Franjo Nakic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic was present at most of the meetings where these allegations were raised, so he was aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Most of the time he let the -- both brigade commanders do the discussions, and he only used to interfere when matters really went out of hand during the meeting, and he had discussions with his battalion commanders during the breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you that Colonel Blaskic had issued orders prohibiting the practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: He did not tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's discuss the burning of houses. We've already seen orders issued by the accused on that subject. Did you see any burning of houses in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I saw a lot of houses burning. I did not see anybody setting any house on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, in the villages that you named, whether all the houses were burned in all those villages at once or whether all of the houses in a particular village were burned on one occasion, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: What do you mean by "at once"? In one day or all in the same hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm suggesting on the same day, were houses in all the villages -- all the houses in all the villages that you saw burned, or did they occur on different days, and within each village? Can you tell us that all the houses in a particular village were burned on one day or, rather, that events were more far-flung, sporadic, and varied?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I can tell for certain villages that it was done in one day or one night, and that some other villages where the majority of the houses were burned in one day and where additional houses were burned because of fighting or because of movements of the frontlines. In other days, then the majority of the houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's compare Ahmici with Rotilj. You visited both?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In Ahmici, all the Muslim homes were burned?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: In Rotilj, approximately five or seven houses were burned in one area where -- well, let's say where you entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that's five or seven houses out of 100 or 200 Muslim homes?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn information concerning what event or incident caused the burning of those seven or eight houses in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I made an investigation on that myself. I went to see the civilians in Rotilj. A lot of Muslim families gathered there. They told me the story. Then I went to one of the local HVO commanders in the area of Rotilj, and he told me a story in the atmosphere of I was -- "I came under fire with my soldiers. One of my soldiers was wounded. I had to return fire, and then I had to burn all seven houses. What else could I do?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. What do you mean "What else"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: He explained it to us in a way that this was the only logical reaction on coming under fire and having one casualty at his own side, so he explained to us that this was a logical reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did he mean that they were being shot at from these seven houses? Were they military zones?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It could have been in a fighting zone. He came under fire, as he told us, one of his soldiers, one of his HVO soldiers, was wounded. He had to return fire, and then he said he had to burn down the houses. It was a logical reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's be perfectly clear, Lieutenant-Colonel. Tell us if you agree with your prior statement on page 7 when you said that you discussed this with the local HVO commander and he said, "He claimed that villagers had opened fire on his troops from a Muslim house and that one HVO soldier had been killed. Fighting had started, and that was when the Muslims had been killed and seven Muslim houses were burnt. The Muslims had handed over 20 weapons and the young men taken to prison. I think this story was accurate." Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's the statement I made in my special report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And do you believe it to be true?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I believe it to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You described a meeting with Mario Cerkez on the 24th of May, 1993, in which he was angry that the BiH army in Kruscica was being reinforced from Opara, and he said something about a threat to burn down all or some portion of Kruscica. Tell me, did Mario Cerkez control Kruscica at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Kruscica was a BiH-controlled village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that true throughout your tour?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think so, yes. We were not able to enter Kruscica every day, of course, but from the beginning and at least in the end, Kruscica was still BiH-controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described a meeting on the 4th of May, 1993, with the Spanish, British, and French ambassadors at which Dzemal Merdan spoke of Muslims being expelled from Gacice; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, is it also correct that -- Colonel Blaskic was not present at that meeting, was he?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't recall that he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, the fighting in Gacice had been some two weeks earlier, around the 20th of April, 1993; is that correct, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any fighting in Gacice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What did Merdan say had occurred in Gacice the prior night, May 3rd, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: As I recall it, Merdan made -- or got the chance to make a lot of complaints in the face of these three ambassadors to explain his view of the whole war so far, and as I recall it, he used, amongst other examples, the example of Gacice where the expelling of Muslims still went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he say who was expelling Muslims? Did he know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have spoken of Franjo Nakic at some length. What did you think of Mr. Nakic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I experienced Mr. Nakic as a moderate man who could have been my father. He gave me that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you think he worked diligently to further the work of the joint operational centre under what were very difficult circumstances?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I learned to know him as a member of the headquarters operational zone, that he supported our work very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned HVO uniforms being in order in Central Bosnia or that HVO soldiers were well-uniformed. Is it correct that you never saw units of the HV or army of the Republic of Croatia in the Lasva or Kiseljak Valleys during your tour?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I never saw units showing the HV insignia. I saw on some occasions individuals wearing this badge with "HV" on it, and I addressed to one of those individuals on one occasion, asking him why he was wearing this, and he said it was hard to obtain uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Implying that he was not a member of the HV, he just had their uniform?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's not literally what he said, but that was the explanation why he used another uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many such persons did you see in the Lasva or Kiseljak Valley wearing at least portions of an HV uniform during your tour?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Approximately five.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you some questions, and this is my final area of inquiry, concerning command and control. You have described a meeting with an individual known as Djuti on the 2nd of June, 1993. I believe you said the prior night Alagic had been stopped at an irregular checkpoint, and it had a car and property taken from him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the checkpoint was irregular, but he was stopped at an HVO checkpoint and then his car and things and his personal weapon were stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, tell me, Lieutenant-Colonel -- I chose my words carefully. In your statement to the Prosecutor at page 16-17, you said: "Earlier that night, Alagic had been stopped at an irregular HVO checkpoint, disarmed, as were his bodyguards." Did you believe the checkpoint to be irregular at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think that the manning of the checkpoint was irregular. The checkpoint itself might have been in a proper place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What do you mean by it was "irregularly manned"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: The way I experienced it was that it was manned by soldiers that were not -- maybe not under control or wore different clothing than normally was done by HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn and conclude from all the facts and circumstances that the individuals who had basically robbed Alagic of this property were acting on self-initiative and not pursuant to orders or directives from the HVO chain of command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. They returned the goods, so maybe they came under pressure of their commander afterwards. I'm not sure if they did it on their own initiative or maybe they were ordered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that Colonel Blaskic apologised to Mr. Alagic through Colonel Duncan for the incident?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree it would be odd for Colonel Blaskic to direct such an incident, direct it to occur?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Would you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree it would be odd for Colonel Blaskic to direct such an incident at a checkpoint and then apologise for it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: If that's the way you describe it, then it would be odd, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, the items taken from Alagic, you learned that they were taken by a group of four men that included two men who had the last name of Tuka, T-U-K-A; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. I've got the names in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were these individuals, the Tuka group, were they HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know. I never met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Nakic ever tell you why he couldn't just order this Tuka group to return the property?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know. He ordered Mr. Djuti and he arranged that they were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he -- well, did you have an interpreter with you when you and Nakic met with Djuti?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the interpreter translate what was said between Nakic and Djuti?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: She translated everything that was openly said during the meeting, not any private discussions, because she used to stay with me and not go with Nakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that Nakic told Djuti to use his influence on the group, referring to the Tuka group, to "calm them down"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That could be true, but Djuti gave me the impression that he was one of the people that stole the things because he made all kinds of excuses why he was allowed to do so and why he was in the full rights to keep the things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you told that Djuti was an extremely powerful and influential person in the Bila-Travnik areas?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I got the impression that he was powerful and he was an impressive person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn, in the course of your dealings with Djuti, that he and a group of his men had freed captives from the Kaonik prison, among other places, through armed assault? Did anyone ever tell you that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: The Kaonik prison was an HVO-held prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Correct. Did anyone tell you that, that Djuti and his men had attacked the Kaonik prison to free one of their comrades at one point during the war?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You spoke of the 7th Muslim brigade not being under the control of the 3rd Korpus until late May 1993. Do you know how many men were in the 7th Muslim brigade and how many soldiers were in the 3rd Corps, excluding the 7th Muslim brigade?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know. I met several of these soldiers belonging to the 7th Muslim brigade. I saw them in Zenica once in a while when we went by car to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why was it necessary to have four local joint commissions rather than one joint operational command which could simply issue orders to -- down the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: There was one joint command in Travnik, operational from, I think, in the middle of May, maybe the beginning of May, and they asked us to organise four local joint commissions to be able to deal with local problems, to be able to arrange to make local arrangements in freedom of movement, in checking on allegations, freedom for Catholic priests in Muslim-held territory or for the imam in HVO-controlled territory, all kinds of local arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Such as observance of the cease-fire which had been agreed to between the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Observance of the cease-fire was not a task for the local joint commission. Both parties agreed on the cease-fire; they should hold to the cease-fire themselves. We were not capable and not asked to check the cease-fire itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Release of prisoners, was that a subject dealt with by the local joint commissions?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. We discussed these matters very often. After a certain -- after a few weeks, we thought we had released the majority of the prisoners, but then new allegations started of new prisons and of more alleged prisons and prisoners being held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that different results were obtained by the different local joint commissions. What were the variables, the factors that affected the relative success or failure of the different local joint commissions?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Let's start with the best commission, according to my opinion. It was the local commission Busovaca where, in the middle of June, we had reached the phase that the representatives of civil government could speak to each other again, where they agreed in making statements for local radio and local television together, where they agreed in freedom of movement for the imam where one of the Muslim fests could be achieved more or less openly, where they agreed on restoring electricity and telephone lines, where there was a certain amount of freedom of movement. So that's the best example. The worst example is Kiseljak where, at the first meeting, HVO representatives failed to come, where Mr. Nakic had to use his influence to order HVO representatives to show up, and, in fact, we never left the phase of complaints. So the few meetings we had in Kiseljak at the Canadian camp were all influenced by complaints from both sides, and there was hardly ever real action undertaken. There was no real result in dealing with local problems at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You've described the level of results in two of the local joint commissions, but my question was: Why were there such variations? Was it because, for example, there was local resistance within the HVO military to obeying orders concerning release of prisoners, et cetera? Was it because there were variations in the degree to which civil authorities wanted to cooperate and work together? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think that's both true. Of course, there are differences in personalities. Some of the commanders were just not willing to discuss things with us. I think both commanders in Busovaca, from HVO and army of BiH, were, for the time being, willing to discuss things with us. They sat together. Quite often we went with them on the ground to check on allegations, we went to this petrol station at Stranje to discuss with local commanders to discuss how the cease-fire could best be implemented. In Vitez, we made with this commission a real exchange of dead bodies, we visited with Mr. Hajdarevic and Mr. Jozic, the two liaison officers, a lot of presence. So in the beginning, the cooperation in Vitez was also quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. You told us the orders of Merdan and Nakic were followed. Let me ask you about an incident that may have been related to you by Lars Baggesen, one of your colleagues. Did he describe how, in Novi Travnik in the middle of April 1993, a military policeman arrested Dzemal Merdan and refused to release him despite the presence of Nakic and direction of Nakic that he should be released? Did Mr. Baggesen describe that to you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You did give us an example in your direct testimony of an order being followed by -- that is an order given by Mr. Nakic being followed by subordinate commanders concerning Kiseljak and Mario Bradara. The example you gave was that Bradara said he had received an order to release prisoners, but he wasn't prepared to obey it because the BiH army had not released their prisoners held in Klokoti, in I think the same region; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I take it Bradara had received a written order to unconditionally release prisoners but had refused?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: At least he did not implement it, and he found an excuse for that because, according to his opinion, the other side didn't do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you seen the order that he received?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the agreement of April 29th, 1993, between Generals Petkovic, Halilovic and so forth, for the unconditional release of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I was present during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So Mr. Bradara, I take it, although he had received an order for unconditional release, he had added a condition to it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Nakic spoke to him at some length; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Nakic was able to persuade him to release BiH army or other civilian prisoners in the Kiseljak barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And did those prisoners, did they appear to be in poor condition?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: They didn't look in a poor condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, at the time, Nakic was able to meet face to face with Bradara and persuade him to follow the order. This was at a time where Nakic was able to get to Kiseljak because he travelled with you; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: We accompanied Mr. Nakic in -- I think it was in our vehicle or maybe in a British armoured vehicle, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And is it correct that after Bradara released the prisoners from Kiseljak barracks, then and only then did the BiH army release some 59 prisoners that they had at Klokoti?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So can we also conclude that the local BiH army commander had not followed orders to unconditionally release the prisoners that he held as well?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: In that case, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let's look at another example that wasn't mentioned in your direct. Two days later, on the 3rd of May, you went to Vitez, I believe, and met with Pero Skopljak, the head of the Commission for Prisoners, and with the mayor of Vitez, a Mr. Santic; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was the role of the Commission for Prisoners in Vitez; can you tell us that initially?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: They didn't fully explain that to me. I met Mr. Skopljak before already, and he introduced himself then as I think the vice-president of HDZ in the area of Vitez, so I was surprised that he introduced himself in a new function later on, and he showed me a long list of people they had in an HVO-controlled prison, and he explained to me that he was head of this new commission and that he was there to organise the release of prisoners on an equal basis from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So this Commission for Prisoners in Vitez was headed by a civil authority or a civilian, Mr. Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there a like entity or institution in Zenica concerned with the subject of prisoner release also headed by a civilian?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I did not meet that commission in Zenica, but I was told that there was a -- I think he's called Bozic who was supposed to be in command or in control of this new commission on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you: On the 3rd of May, did Skopljak and Santic, would you say it's accurate to describe what occurred at that meeting as follows: "They were a pair of hard-liners, and they did not want to release prisoners. They said that they had received orders to release the prisoners, but they refused to do so." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's accurate. That was my opinion at that period. That's what I wrote in my diary that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The next day, the 4th of May, there was a joint operational command meeting, and is it correct that Ambassador Thebault said at that meeting that he would try and negotiate with the mayor of Zenica, Mr. Spahic, and with Mr. Santic over the release of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I recall that Mr. Thebault more or less took over this problem of release of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And in the same context, did Mr. Nakic complain that there was no success with prisoner release in Vitez and Zenica because the civil authorities were not cooperating?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, he complained about that, but the prisoners, as far as I know, were held in a cellar in Vitez under the cinema, and the other prisoners were held in Dubravica, and I visited both prisons and they were guarded by HVO soldiers, not by Mr. Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Obviously, Mr. Skopljak can only be in one place at one time.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's clear. But he was in charge of this commission, and he was not in charge of guarding the prisoners themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you. You mentioned a moment ago the formation of the Kiseljak joint commission, and I'd ask you to think about that subject on the issue of command and control. Do you know, had the Kiseljak HVO brigade been ordered on approximately the 22nd of April to form a joint commission in a joint order issued by Dzemal Merdan and Franjo Nakic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Nakic told me, that he issued the order to all his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist? And if this exhibit could be provided to the witness and distributed? Mr. Registrar, will this be Defence Exhibit 152?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's right, it is D152.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a copy of an order, with appropriate translations, signed by Dzemal Merdan and Franjo Nakic, among other things ordering the BiH army and the HVO in the towns of Vitez, Travnik, Busovaca, and Kiseljak to form local joint commissions; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And it's dated the 22nd of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It says so in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then let's take that as our basis for analysing this question and proceed to the 10th of May, 1993. You went to CANBAT in Visoko for a meeting, a planned meeting, of the Kiseljak joint commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't recall whether it was the 10th of May, but we had one of those meetings, one of these start-up meetings, in Visoko at CANBAT.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that at this first start-up meeting, the HVO delegates did not appear?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. We arranged transport for these delegates through the Canadian battalion, and they did not show up with the HVO representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So they had been ordered on the 22nd of April to form the local joint commission, but on the 10th of May, they didn't show up for the meeting. Did you then go to Kiseljak with Mr. Nakic to try and "move them off the dime," if you will?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we went to Kiseljak on that very day, but I recall that we did go to Kiseljak maybe on the second occasion to speak to the local HVO commanders and to explain to them the need for a local joint commission and the use we could be to them as well to organise this local joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if this refreshes your memory. It's on page 11 of your statement under the 10th of May, 1993: "We went on to Kiseljak to try and locate these members. We met Bozic," a reference to brigade commander Mijo Bozic, "and he said that he had received orders to establish the local commission but he said he was waiting for further orders." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think that was on the same day then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that a way of a subordinate commander -- a way a subordinate commander might state "I haven't complied with the order," in effect?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, if he states that he got the first order and still doesn't comply, then he's just disobeying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And then did Nakic discuss this with Mr. Bozic and order Bozic to get on with it, to get on with the work and form the commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, and later on the commission was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, two days later, you again went to Kiseljak for the joint commission meeting, this is the 12th of May, 1993, and am I correct that again the HVO representatives did not show up?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. This mission -- this next meeting was organised at the Canadian base in Kiseljak itself, called Camp Paardeberg, and it's only a few kilometres from the HVO headquarters, so we again went to the HVO headquarters, and Nakic, according to my knowledge, again explained to them why they had to show up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you surprised that these HVO officers in Kiseljak were so brazenly defying Nakic's instructions as well his written order of the 22nd of April?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, this was already the third occasion where they refused to obey orders which they actually had received, according to their own statements, and, well, finally Nakic succeeded in ordering these people to show up and they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let's return to Vitez. On the 24th of May, 1993, there was a local commission meeting in Vitez, and I believe this is the meeting in which Mario Cerkez made remarks about burning in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Would you say the date again?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Is that the day when the ambassadors were present?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, it's not, according to your earlier statement. What I would like to ask concerning this meeting is whether or not, at this meeting, there were HVO representatives present who said that "They had orders from Mr. Skopljak to stop the work of the commission." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who was that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It was a very unclear situation to us since the local joint commission Vitez more or less seemed to come to an end. We didn't like that, and we tried to find out how this was arranged or what was the reason why we couldn't continue our work. The first explanation was from the side of the HVO members of the local commission that it was unsafe for the whole commission to travel in the area. The second explanation, maybe on the same day or a day later, was that we should transfer our military commission into a civil commission; and as I recall it, that was relating to this, let's call it an order or words of Mr. Skopljak to stop the military part of the commission and change it into a civil commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At this meeting on the 24th of May, 1993, did Mr. Nakic, Colonel Blaskic's representative to the joint operational command, appeal to the commanders present to stop the war activities and have an unconditional cease-fire, but there was no willingness from the local HVO to make things work? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I remember that I made that statement according to my notes from this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, you tried to resuscitate the Vitez joint commission; is that not true? You tried to have another meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. I tried to restart it at the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Nakic went with you, he was organised and waiting, but the BiH army side cancelled, saying they were too busy with their military operation in Zepce; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether Mr. Merdan could not show up or whether the local BiH commanders could not show up. I think it must have been Mr. Merdan since the local commanders didn't have anything to do with an area outside their area of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And he couldn't come because at the time the BiH army was attacking the HVO in Zepce; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were attacking there. He was busy dealing with Zepce items or Zepce things in his headquarters in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Nakic tell you at the meeting you had with him -- I guess it was just the two of you -- on the 30th of June, 1993, that the BiH army had attacked the HVO on three sides in Zepce, and that the HVO plus 40.000 refugees had been forced to flee?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's what he told me, and later on the BRITBAT did examinations on that, and it appeared to be something else than Mr. Nakic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. That concludes my examination. Thank you for your patience. I would like to offer into evidence Exhibits D141, D144, D145, D146, D150, and D152. If there is an objection to D152, I would ask to be permitted to ask a few further foundational questions of the witness to lay the foundation and to authenticate that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon? There's a proverb in French: "Silence is consent."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I can assist, perhaps? A couple of these exhibits are the stills of the video which counsel may not have a copy of, so there may not be documents corresponding to every number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify those, counsel, for us, which are the stills? We have no objection to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would need the assistance of the registrar to do so, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will remind you, all of the documents which were presented, D141 and 141A were documents which were presented before another witness for the first time on the 29th of June before Mark Bower, and that was represented again today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objection to D141.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D144 was the document -- rather, a still image taken from a video, 409, that was presented yesterday evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objection to any of the stills taken from videos.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D146 is the same thing, that's also taken from video 270; document 145 was a document read by Mr. Hayman which comes from the Council of Europe document that was read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 145. 146 is the still photo. You said you have no objections to that. There was also D147 A and B, D147 A and B, D149. These are not being tendered, I understand, and then there was D150. I believe that's an order, if I'm not mistaken. As well as D151.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objection to 150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. No objections, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And document 152? There is still 152.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I see we have somewhat of a problem here. It is 12.40. Now, I first want to turn to you, Mr. Harmon. Do you intend -- how much time do you expect for your redirect? Please tell us very objectively how much time you feel you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Probably in the area of 30 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, we are going to then adjourn. The witness will return to receive questions from the Prosecution and also the Judges have questions for the witness, and therefore, we'll also need to take the time necessary for those questions. Of course, the 20 minutes remaining will not be taken as part of those minutes allotted to the Prosecution. Therefore, we're going to ask the witness to return, but I'd like to know, Mr. Harmon, and also the witness, when can the witness return? Can he come back on Monday, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Monday would be fine. Monday suits me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We thank the witness, therefore, for making this contribution. Mr. Harmon, then, we will resume on Monday with the witness. That's the best solution, I believe. Are we in agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. On these conditions, we will now adjourn, and we would also like to thank the witness for his contribution. Have a very nice weekend. The Chamber shall resume at 2.30 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 12.43 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of July, 1998, at 2.30 p.m.
